title: Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus
snippet:
As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreak

The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus. [...] Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, the Bundibugyo strain of the virus has spread faster than any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in 2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRC were infected. [...] At 3,360 confirmed cases, the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas.

title: The Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak Congo Declared In May Likely Began In January
snippet:
Seven days later Congo declared an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus, an Ebola species for which there is no licensed vaccine and no specific treatment. It is now the second-largest on record, with 3,802 confirmed cases and 1,707 deaths as of August 3.

Dhenyo was not being evasive. He was describing what his surveillance system could see, which by then was almost four months behind what was happening.

## Five Hundred Cases Nobody Counted [...] Eastern Congo's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, now the second-largest on record, was officially declared in May but likely began four months earlier. On May 8, a local health official in Mongbwalu dismissed an epidemic, noting varied symptoms and drug use, unaware of the true scale. A WHO-funded field study later uncovered over 500 suspected cases between mid-January and the declaration, including 13 health worker deaths and a significant increase in burials. The earliest identified death was a [...] They counted more than 500 suspected cases between mid-January and the declaration. Thirteen front-line health workers died. The cemetery was managing as many as twenty burials in a day.

The first of those deaths they could date was a fifty-year-old woman on the outskirts of town who died on January 25 after vomiting blood. Her mother died six days later. Her husband fell ill and recovered.
